title: The AI Credibility Gap: When Confidence Outruns Evidence in CX
summary: New research from Metric Sherpa and Sprinklr: nine in 10 CX and marketing leaders say AI delivered, but barely one in four can quantify it. Here's what the few with proof do differently.

# The AI Credibility Gap: When Confidence Outruns Evidence in CX


November 19, 2026 • 5 MIN READ


Authors


Naveen Mahadevan is a content strategist, writer and editor with experience spanning journalism, photography and B2B SaaS marketing. At Sprinklr, he writes about customer experience, social media, AI and modern marketing, turning complex business ideas into stories that are accessible and thought-provoking. His work blends research, empathy and storytelling to help leaders see beyond the technology and focus on the people behind it.


[View full bio](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/author/naveen-mahadevan/)


If you ask a room full of CX leaders whether their AI is working, you'll get a near-unanimous yes. But as soon as you ask them to put a number on it, you’ll be hard-pressed for an answer.


That's the pattern highlighted in “Show Your Work,” a new study report by Metric Sherpa in partnership with Sprinklr.


92% of leaders whose organizations run customer-facing AI say it met or exceeded expectations. Only 27% say they can quantify the result precisely using records or reports. The study surveyed 807 U.S. marketing, service, and CX practitioners in September 2026, all of them people who define, fund, run, or review customer-facing AI programs.


The finding isn't that AI fails. It's that confidence has run well ahead of evidence. The report calls this the AI credibility gap.


Table of Contents

- Where the gap opens
- What the disciplined few do differently

##


**The results look almost too good**


The survey asked about eight categories of business metrics, from handling time to revenue to risk. In every single one, fewer than 4% said performance got worse. More than one in five respondents (22%) said all eight improved.


Now look at what sits behind those answers. When the survey asked people to enter the actual metric, its starting value and its current value, only about three in ten gave a complete answer. One respondent named email open rate over 12 months, moving from an estimated 13.5% to 17.2%. Another typed "Estimate" into every field.


Here's the detail that should make any CX leader stop. People who said they could quantify their result precisely produced a complete number at almost exactly the same rate as everyone else (27.3% versus 27.2%). Feeling sure about the result and being able to show the number turned out to be two very different things.


##


**Gains nobody was measuring**


So where are all these improvements coming from? Part of the answer lies in what teams were tracking before launch.


85% of respondents reported improvement in at least one metric their organization did not track before AI went live. Some teams may have started measuring after launch or pulled figures from another source. Still, the pattern is hard to miss: the improvements people claim go well beyond what they were measuring at the start.


The clearest case is the leap from speed to savings. Among leaders who say AI made work faster, 67.4% also say it cut costs. Only 32.1% of that group tracked cost before launch.


That's a big leap on thin evidence. A saved hour is real, but it only reaches the P&L sheet when someone decides what that hour is for: a leaner staffing plan, harder cases, or better service levels. Until that decision is made and written down, the savings on the slide deck don’t really translate into reality.


##


**Where the gap opens**


Thin evidence after launch usually traces back to a thin trail before it. Nearly every organization knew what it wanted from AI. Very few turned that intent into a record anyone could check later.


The steepest drop comes between setting expectations and defining success metrics, from 69% to 26%. Also, only 17% of organizations assign a named owner for AI business outcomes, which makes it the least common of the eight practices the study measured.


Then there's the question of expectations.


23% of respondents said their organization set none before launch. Yet 85% of that group still say AI met or exceeded those expectations. One customer service manager in retail put it plainly: "We had no expectations really. My boss just thought it was a neat toy that customers might like."


When there's no bar, almost any welcome improvement feels like a win. And with 18% saying leadership has never asked for proof, few teams are pushed to set one. The trouble starts later, when someone with a budget asks how you got there.


##


**What the disciplined few do differently**


Is anyone getting this right? Yes, though not many.


Only 4.5% of organizations report six or more of the eight measurement practices in the study. That small group of 24 respondents says it can quantify results precisely 63% of the time, nearly three times the rate of organizations reporting zero or one practice (23%). The sample size is small, so treat that gap as directional, but the direction is hard to ignore.


Across the wider data, three things show up again and again alongside stronger proof.


1. **An owner.** Teams with a named outcome owner report precise results twice as often (46% versus 23%).
2. **Expectations.** Teams that set expectations before launch report precise results twice as often (32.1% versus 16.4%).
3. **Time.** Deployments that have been live for two years or more report precise results at 43%, versus 25.0% for newer ones. Yet 58% of live deployments are less than a year old. For most teams, the proof is still being built.


The report turns these patterns into five disciplines, each built around one question:


1. **Outcome:** What changes for the customer and the business, beyond hours saved?
2. **Owner:** Who owns the result?
3. **Baseline:** What did performance look like before AI?
4. **Comparison:** How do we isolate AI's contribution?
5. **Review:** What triggers a decision to scale, change or stop?


The survey can't show which practice causes better proof. That's exactly why the disciplines are framed as questions: each one is something you can ask, and test, in your own AI program.


##


**Start with one application**


You don't need a new measurement program for every AI tool you run. Pick one customer-facing AI application that matters, whether that's a self-service bot or agent assist on live chats, and put it through the report's eight-question scorecard. Can you point to a goal, a baseline, an owner, a review rhythm, a comparison, a change log, decision criteria, and a leadership readout? Each Yes needs a document or a person behind it.


Then use the report's 90-day plan to close whatever you marked No, starting with the owner.
